claims.text: An equiatomic Ti–Ni–Hf–Zr high-entropy alloy can be produced in a single-phase solid-solution state by conventional processing.
Aging at 600–700 °C for 2–4 hours followed by rapid quenching will induce Ni3Ti precipitation in the target Ti–Ni-based alloy.
The aging treatment will produce nanoscale Ni3Ti precipitates.
The resulting Ni3Ti precipitates will be uniformly dispersed throughout the matrix.
The resulting Ni3Ti precipitates will be coherent with the solid-solution matrix.
Nanoscale coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby provide precipitation strengthening.
Ni3Ti precipitates restrict grain-boundary sliding in the target alloy.
Ni3Ti precipitates act as obstacles to elevated-temperature creep deformation.
The aging treatment will significantly increase elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The aging treatment will significantly improve creep resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated as-cast or as-quenched baseline is a single-phase solid solution without aging-induced precipitates.
The intervention is expected to be beneficial in Ti–Ni-based high-entropy alloys in which Ti and Ni are primary constituents.
The intervention's benefits are expected during testing above 600 °C or under prolonged extreme-environment exposure.
Substantially different compositions or processing histories may alter the treatment response.
Over-aging or precipitate coarsening may reduce the mechanical-property improvement.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on optimization of the aging parameters.
Elevated-temperature tensile and creep testing against an untreated control can test the predicted mechanical improvement.
TEM and XRD can be used to assess whether aging produced the proposed Ni3Ti precipitates.

contradictions.description: The conditions include testing at temperatures greater than or equal to 600 °C, whereas the boundary states that applicability is above 600 °C, creating a minor inconsistency at exactly 600 °C.
